title: Aids to Reflection; and, The Confessions of an Inquiring Spirit
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
public_title: Why Your Doubt Feels Like Truth Part 1 🧠
hook: You feel certain when you are confused.

sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You feel certain when you are confused. Two centuries ago, Coleridge called this the 'opium of the mind'. In 1970s cognitive research, this was finally mapped. You think your feeling of certainty is proof. It is not. Your brain creates a smooth feeling called 'fluency'. The result? That smoothness tricks you into truth. That's it. So why do we trust our gut? Because it saves energy. What did the researchers find? Daniel Kahneman showed in 1974 that people judge truth by how easily information flows in their head. This was not just one lab. Studies across cultures confirm 'processing fluency'. We see the same bias in ancient texts. Coleridge warned that doubt is not a flaw. It is a tool. He said the mind must break its own certainties. Does it still hold today? Yes. When you feel sure, check the facts. Not the feeling. So next time you argue online, remember your brain is lazy. You feel certain when you are confused.

claims.claim: People judge truth by how easily information flows in their head (processing fluency).
Doubt is a necessary tool for the mind to break its own certainties.
